sections.h2: Who values a Brownsville house, and who collects the tax?
sections.html:
The Cameron Appraisal District sets the value, and the Cameron County Tax Assessor-Collector sends one combined bill covering the county, the schools, the cities and the special districts. The two are often mixed up. The appraisal district sits in San Benito, has no tax amounts and takes no payments, so questions about what you owe go to the tax office.

The appraisal district's hours run 7:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Monday through Thursday and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday, and its site has a property search, a map search and a Truth in Taxation portal. Texas has no state property tax, so every rate on a Brownsville bill comes from a local body.

sections.h2: What rates did Brownsville's taxing units list for 2026?
sections.html:
The county's Truth in Taxation summary prints a rate per $100 of taxable value for each unit that touches most Brownsville homes. The figures below set 2026 beside 2025.

Rates per $100 of taxable value, from the Cameron County Truth in Taxation summary

City of Brownsville$0.603504$0.603504
Brownsville ISD$0.771600$0.831460
Cameron County$0.424393$0.424393

Brownsville Navigation District$0.025589$0.025589

The city line splits into $0.353581 for maintenance and operations and $0.249923 for debt. Its no-new-revenue rate reads $0.563407 and its voter-approval rate $0.613440. The school district's line has fallen a long way from the $1.208690 it printed for 2022.

Drainage districts, municipal utility districts and other special districts add their own levy, so read every line on your bill. The city has also posted a notice of intent to issue certificates of obligation up to $27,000,000, to be paid from property tax and landfill surplus revenue, and it lists $355,576,000 in outstanding debt principal. Those debt numbers help explain the debt portion of the city rate.

sections.h2: What does a Brownsville owner owe after January 31?
sections.html:
Bills mail around October 1 and are due January 31. On February 1 a six percent penalty and one percent interest attach, per the Comptroller, and the county tax office describes it as 7 percent in penalty and interest.

  • The penalty climbs a point each month and reaches 12 percent on July 1.
  • A private collection attorney can add up to 20 percent.
  • Under Tax Code 33.011 an owner may ask for a waiver, generally by paying within 21 days of learning the bill was late.

Homeowners who are 65 or older, disabled, or a disabled veteran or a surviving spouse can split a homestead bill into quarterly payments due January 31, March 31, May 31 and July 31. The office posts its online fees: $1.00 for an internet check of $5,000 or less, $3.00 above that, and 3 percent on cards.

sections.h2: Which exemptions can Brownsville homeowners claim?
sections.html:
A residence homestead removes $140,000 of value from school taxes, and owners 65 or older or disabled get $60,000 more against school taxes. A 10 percent yearly cap limits the appraisal of a homestead.

The Cameron Appraisal District adds that a senior's school tax ceiling can transfer to a new homestead in Texas, and that it rises if you add a pool, garage or room. An owner cannot claim both over-65 and disabled status in the same year, and both spouses must apply and show proof of Texas residency.

The Brownsville Navigation District, known as the Port of Brownsville, approved a full homestead exemption for qualifying owners who are 65 or older or disabled. The city's September 2026 notice says it begins with the 2027 tax year and covers Brownsville, Rancho Viejo, Los Fresnos, Indian Lake and Starbase. Disabled veterans may get partial exemptions, and a 100 percent rating earns a full one. Apply to the appraisal district by April 30, using Form 50-114 for the homestead types.

sections.h2: How does the Cameron Appraisal District handle a protest?
sections.html:
A protest must be written. Mail it, deliver it, fax it to (956) 399-6969 or email protest@cameroncad.org. Mailed protests can go to PO Box 1010, San Benito, TX 78586, and must be postmarked by the deadline: May 15 or 30 days after the value notice, whichever is later. No official form is needed, only the owner, the property and a statement that you disagree.

  • Informal hearings with an appraiser: walk-ins run from April 14 to May 16, first come first served, and requested ones happen by phone.
  • Formal hearing: usually three members, about 15 minutes, with at least 15 days of notice.
  • One postponement is allowed without a showing of cause if you named no agent.
  • An appeal can go to district court, binding arbitration under limited conditions, or in Cameron County to the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

The board decides market value as of January 1 and nothing about service quality or rates. Without a timely protest neither the appraiser nor the board can change the value. The district reappraises every property at least once every three years, and it need not mail a notice when value rises by $1,000 or less.

sections.h2: Where did Brownsville come from, and what do the Census numbers say?
sections.html:
Brownsville sits at the southern tip of Texas, across the Rio Grande from Matamoros, and is the county seat. The Handbook of Texas ties it to 1848, when Charles Stillman and a partner laid out a town beside Fort Brown. The county seat designation came January 13, 1849. Voters created the Brownsville Navigation District in December 1928 to build the ship channel, and the port opened May 15, 1936. The college district that still levies a tax began partnering with the University of Texas at Brownsville in 1991.

  • 2025 estimate: 192,957 residents, up 3.6 percent from the 2020 base.
  • Typical owned home, 2020 to 2024 survey: $139,900.
  • 61.7 percent of homes are lived in by their owners.
  • Typical rent: $923, with 3.13 people per household.
  • Land area: 131.53 square miles.

sections.h2: What else should a Brownsville seller know about records and tax?
sections.html:
The title company asks the tax office for a payoff and settles the balance when the sale funds. The lien attaches each January 1, and the owner on that date stays personally liable after a later sale.

Copies of deeds, plats and mortgage records come from the Cameron County Clerk at 835 E. Levee St., Brownsville, (956) 544-0815, not from the appraisal district. A change of ownership needs a recorded instrument or volume and page. Mobile homes need a Statement of Ownership and Location before the land and home combine on one bill. Land taken out of agricultural use triggers a rollback tax owed by whoever holds title then.

If a bill is already late, ask the Cameron tax office about a payment agreement. The Comptroller says some collectors allow up to 36 months and that a plan is required for a residence homestead. After a collection suit starts, court costs join the bill. Foreclosure sales are public auctions with no statewide list, so look for notices from the county clerk and tax office.

faqs.q: Which Brownsville taxing unit has the highest 2026 rate?
faqs.a: Brownsville ISD, at $0.771600 per $100 of taxable value, ahead of the city at $0.603504 and the county at $0.424393 in the county's summary table.

faqs.q: When do Brownsville property taxes become late?
faqs.a: February 1 for a bill unpaid after January 31. Penalty and interest start then, and the penalty climbs to 12 percent by July 1.

faqs.q: Can I email a Brownsville appraisal protest?
faqs.a: Yes. The appraisal district accepts written protests by email at protest@cameroncad.org, by fax, by mail or by hand. Mailed protests must carry a postmark by the deadline.

faqs.q: Do older Brownsville homeowners get anything from the port district?
faqs.a: The Brownsville Navigation District approved a full homestead exemption for owners 65 or older or disabled, starting with the 2027 tax year, applied for through the appraisal district.

faqs.q: Where do I get a copy of my Brownsville deed?
faqs.a: From the Cameron County Clerk, 835 E. Levee St., Brownsville, (956) 544-0815. The appraisal district does not hold deeds.
